list.listitem: Carcinoid tumors are rare neuroendocrine tumors with an indolent course whose embryologic origins reflect their primary occurrence in the gut. B

Initial symptoms may include bowel dysmotility syndromes, valvular cardiac disease, and respiratory symptoms refractory to traditional treatments; many are discovered coincidentally at surgery for another indication. C
5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) and serum chromogranin A are the recommended initial tests for patients with vasoactive symptoms who are suspected of having carcinoid tumors. C
Carcinoid tumors have a high association with secondary primary malignancies that should provoke further diagnostic evaluation. C
Treatment choices are complex and predicated on the location of the tumor and the extent of metastasis at the time of diagnosis (). Surgery remains the cornerstone of treatment. B

background.definition: Carcinoid tumors describe neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) which arise from aerodigestive tissues and have well or moderately differentiated histology, the latter also called atypical carcinoid tumor. Carcinoid tumors are rare, slow-growing tumors that derivated from the neural crest origine.

list.listitem: NETs represent approximately 0.5% of all cancers.Data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER), the age-adjusted incidence rate increased 6.4 fold from 1973 to 2012.
In patients with known carcinoid tumors of the intestinal tract, the rate of second primary malignancies ranges from 12% to 46%.
These cancers are often more aggressive and have a higher mortality rate than carcinoid itself.

Genetic predisposition: Although there are a variety of genes known to be involved in neuroendocrine tumorigenesis, mutations in the multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) gene remain the most common forms of genetic predisposition.
Smoking: There is evidence that smoking is a risk factor for small bowel carcinoid tumors.
Carcinoid tumors are dispersed from neuroectodermal cells and found most often in the GI tract ().
The most common locations are the duodenum, terminal ileum, and the appendix.

Carcinoid tumors produce and secrete a number of substances, most notably 5-hydroxy tryptophan and 5-hydroxy indole acetic acid, as well as chromogranin A and C, growth hormone, and other related substances.
In a large cohort study, dietary fiber/whole grain intake was generally associated with a lower risk of small intestinal cancer.
Symptoms of carcinoid tumors may include bowel dysmotility syndromes, valvular cardiac disease, and respiratory symptoms refractory to traditional treatments. C
Carcinoid tumors are often discovered at the time of surgery for another indication. C
5-HIAA and serum chromogranin A are the recommended initial tests for patients with vasoactive symptoms who are suspected of having carcinoid tumors. C
A multimodal approach for imaging is recommended and may include CT, MRI, somatostatin scintography using indium-111-labeled octreotide, endoscopic ultrasonography and PET CT. C
Carcinoid tumors have a high association with secondary primary malignancies that should provoke further diagnostic evaluation. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Flushing: menopause, pheochromocytoma, mastocytosis, benign cutaneous flushing, medullary thyroid cancer, food, and drugs
Wheezing: asthma, anaphylaxis, pulmonary edema, and bronchial foreign body
Diarrhea: gastroenteritis, inflammatory bowel disease, infectious colitis, laxative abuse, and irritable bowel
Heart valve symptoms: rheumatic heart disease, subacute bacterial endocarditis, dilated cardiomyopathy, ischemic heart disease with papillary muscle dysfunction

list.listitem: The carcinoid syndrome may include flushing, watery and explosive diarrhea, tachycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, telangiectasia, and right-sided heart disease.
Only 5% to 7% of patients with carcinoid tumors will display the clinical features of this syndrome, which may not appear until the tumor has metastasized to the lungs or liver.
The patient's symptoms depend to some extent on the location of the tumor ().
Bowel dysmotility symptoms can be a manifestation of carcinoid tumors and are often treated according to different presumed causalities, which may lead to a delayed diagnosis and treatment.
Measure the urinary excretion of 5-HIAA and serum chromogranin A in patients with vasoactive symptoms.
Fasting plasma 5-HIAA concentrations provide a more convenient screening test and overcome logistical issues associated with 24-hour urine collections.

A multimodal imaging approach is recommended that may include barium enemas or CT studies to detect gut mucosal thickening, a submucosal mass, or luminal narrowing. Gallium 68 PET /CT scan is more sensitive than F-FDG 18 (90% versus 71%) to detect pulmonary carcinoid.
CT scanning may show the mesenteric extension of tumors and liver masses with endoscopic ultrasonography as a option.
Meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) is a structural analog to norepinephrine and I-labeled MIBG can be used for the detection of neuroendocrine tumors.
Carcinoid tumors have a high association with secondary primary malignancies that should provoke further diagnostic evaluation.
The diagnosis of carcinoid tumors is often coincidental, with the tumor discovered at the time of surgery for another reason.
When there are symptoms suggestive of the release of vasoactive substances (carcinoid syndrome), measure the urinary excretion of 5-HIAA and serum chromogranin A levels.

In a study of patients with carcinoid heart disease, N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide at a cut-off level of 260 pg/mL had a sensitivity and specificity for detection of 0.92 and 0.91, respectively.
For patients with symptoms of bowel dysmotility syndromes, CT, and MRI may be helpful.

In 1 study of symptomatic patients suspected of having a small bowel neoplasm, MR Enteroclysis enabled correct detection of 19 small-bowel neoplasms, including 3 carcinoid tumors. The overall sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy in identifying patients with small-bowel lesions were 86%, 98%, and 97%, respectively.
Surgery remains the cornerstone of treatment and provides the only chance of a cure (). B
Biological treatment includes cytotoxic agents such as somatostatin analogs and interferon alpha, which should be applied in slow-growing neoplasms. B
Other cytoreductive procedures include radiofrequency ablation, laser treatment, and chemoembolization. B

Treatment decisions for patients with carcinoid tumors are complex and related to the location of the primary tumor and whether metastasis has occurred. The goal of therapy should be curative when possible, while maintaining a good quality of life.
Octreotide (a somatostatin analog) is the most common drug therapy and may be used in combination with specific chemotherapeutic regimes or alpha interferon.
The RADIANT4 trial led to recent approval in the US of everolimus as a treatment for typical and atypical carcinoid to reduce the risk of progression.

Biological treatment includes cytotoxic agents such as somatostatin analogs and interferon alpha, which should be applied in slow-growing neoplasms. A randomized trial found that interferon alpha reduced tumor growth in patients with disseminated midgut carcinoid tumors, with a trend toward better survival (56.8% vs 36.6%).

177Lu-DOTA0-Tyr-octreotate ("177Lu-Dotatate") allows targeted delivery of radionuclides. A clinical trial randomized 229 patients with metastatic, well-differentiated midgut neuroendocrine tumors to 177 Lu-Dotatate plus long-acting repeatable (LAR) octreotide or LAR octreotide alone for 8 weeks. The rate of progression free survival at 20 months was 65% in the intervention group and only 11% in the comparison group (p <0.001, NNT = 2). There were also fewer deaths in the intervention group (14 vs 26, p = 0.004, NNT = 10).

Management of symptoms and complications (heart disease, flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing) is important; octreotide is the most useful therapy for this purpose. A systematic review found that most carcinoid crises could be managed with doses of octreotide in the range of 25 to 500 mcg IV. Rarely, much higher doses have been reported (up to 54,000 mcg) although outcome data were not reported.

For flushing, avoid precipitating foods and consider a 5-HT3 antagonist or interferon; hepatic artery embolization may be necessary in addition to octreotide. Antidiarrheal agents aid in symptomatic control as adjuvants to antitumor chemotherapeutic agents. Wheezing responds to traditional bronchodilators while the primary tumor is being treated.
In the presence of heart disease, diuretics, and valvular replacement may be required.
When a resectable tumor mass is found, it should be removed surgically, regardless of whether it has been previously associated with any symptoms.

Radiation with somatostatin analogs can also be a helpful adjunct, as can laser ablation and chemoembolization. Image guided ablation is mostly helpful with small volume tumors and when used in combination with resection. Ablation can also be used as part of cytoreduction in patients with metastatic disease.

In patients with a primary midgut carcinoid tumor and unresectable liver metastases, resection of the primary carcinoid tumor was associated with longer survival although the quality of evidence was limited.
Partial hepatic resection can reduce tumor burden and in a retrospective series of 169 patients there were no documented cases of carcinoid crisis.
A systematic review found little evidence to support the decision to perform lobectomy versus sub-lobar resection in patients with peripheral carcinoid tumors of the lung.

Analysis of the natural history of pulmonary carcinoid from the SEER database over a 20 year period demonstrated a benefit in disease specific survival at 5 years from surgery versus no surgery. The indolent natural history and good overall survival even without resection, though, would support a policy of observation in those patients for whom surgical resection would be a high risk procedure.

Analysis of 6,673 cases of resected pulmonary carcinoid tumours from the National Cancer Database examined the benefit of adjuvant chemotherapy post-operatively. This was not found to be beneficial in typical carcinoids but may have some benefit in stage III atypical carcinoids.
External beam radiotherapy is recommended to relieve metastatic bone pain.
Carcinoid tumors are complex and often require consultation with endocrinologists, oncologists, and surgeons.
Carcinoid tumors are relatively uncommon neoplasms and most of them are found in the small bowel. B
Carcinoids in the ileum tend to be more aggressive and carry a poorer prognosis than carcinoids in other locations. B
Typical carcinoid tumor of the lung has a fairly good prognosis (approximately 88% 5-year survival), whereas atypical carcinoid has a 5-year survival of approximately 50%.
Tumors found in the appendix are found at a younger age and at an early stage; they rarely metastasize and have an excellent prognosis. B
Advanced carcinoid tumor remains incurable. B

Authors of a proposed staging system for colonic carcinoid tumors, based on 2459 cases from the National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, identified age, size, depth of invasion, lymph node involvement, distant metastasis, and location as significant factors for prognosis. Five-year survival rates for the 4 created stages were 97% for stage I (13% of the total cases), 69% for stage II (32% of total cases), 21% for stage III (12% of total cases), and 17% for stage IV (43% of total cases). A similar TNM (tumor, node, metastasis) system was derived for small intestine carcinoid tumors based on 6380 patients with 5-year survival rates of 96%, 87%, 74%, and 43% for stages I through IV, respectively.
Although rare, carcinoid tumors are 1 of the 2 most common primary lung malignancies in children.

feature.caption: Treatment Options for Patients with Malignant Carcinoid Tumors.
feature.feature_body:
Carcinoid Tumor
Surgical resection, if possible:
Hepatic metastases dominant: long-acting somatostatin analogs; hepatic artery embolization or ligation with or without interferon, with or without chemotherapy
Systemic spread: chemotherapy or interferon or long-acting somatostatin analogs
Carcinoid Syndrome
Systematic progression through treatment options:
Heart disease: diuretics, long-acting somatostatin analogs, and occasional valvular replacement
Flushing: avoid precipitating food and alcohol; 5-HT3-receptor antagonist; long-acting somatostatin analogs; interferon; hepatic artery embolization or ligation with or without interferon, with or without chemotherapy
Diarrhea: antidiarrheal agents; 5-HT3-receptor antagonist; long-acting somatostatin analogs; interferon; hepatic artery embolization or ligation with or without interferon, with or without chemotherapy
Wheezing: selective bronchodilators; long-acting somatostatin analogs; interferon; hepatic artery embolization or ligation with or without interferon, with or without chemotherapy
5-HT-3 denotes serotonin receptor subtype 5-hydroxytryptamine-3. Adapted from Robertson RG, Geiger WJ, Davis NB. Carcinoid tumors. Am Fam Phys 2006;74:429-434.
